Private DNS is set to %1$s, so every lookup leaves the phone encrypted, straight to that server. Malachi never sees one, and nothing is being filtered. Set Private DNS to Off or Automatic for filtering to work.

Private DNS is set to Automatic. Filtering works normally — Android only encrypts when the server on the other end offers it, and Malachi does not. The trade is that while Malachi is on, your lookups are forwarded unencrypted.

“Block connections without VPN” is on. Malachi only carries lookups, so Android is dropping everything else and the phone has no working connection. Turn that setting off; always-on VPN on its own is fine and is what you want.

How refusals are answered, and where the lookups that are allowed through are sent.
What an app is told when Malachi refuses a domain. If something behaves oddly, this is the first thing to try.
The app believes the name resolved and fails to connect. Most ad code gives up quietly. Recommended.
Cleaner in theory, but some apps read it as a broken network and retry in a loop.
Unambiguous when you are working out what is happening; some apps respond by trying a different server.
A lookup Malachi allows still has to be answered by somebody. This is who answers it.
Follows the Wi-Fi or mobile network you are on. The safest default.
Type the addresses of the DNS servers you want to use.
IP addresses only, separated by commas. Names are not accepted — looking one up would need the very server you are setting.
Let apps reach a network they ask for

Android Auto, casting and captive portals need to talk to a device directly, and Android refuses that to every app while a VPN is on unless this is allowed. An app that deliberately asks is then not filtered — nothing that serves an advert does, but turning this off is the strictest this filter gets.

Nearly every app asks the phone where to find a site, and Malachi answers those. A few skip the question and go straight to an address written inside them, which is how an advert gets through anyway. This is how far Malachi goes after them — each step catches more and risks more.
The safest setting: nothing on this phone can break because of Malachi. The handful of apps that dodge keep their adverts.

Covers the apps that go straight to the DNS servers this network gave your phone, which is where nearly all of them go. Your own router is deliberately left alone, so it keeps answering everything else. It rarely breaks anything.

Also covers the big public services some apps carry inside them, like Google\'s 8.8.8.8. Catches the most, and is the one that occasionally stops an app working — if something breaks, come back and take a step down.
Your rules and your chosen lists, in a file you keep. Everything else rebuilds itself on a new phone; these do not.
You have changes that aren\'t in any copy yet.

To a chat, a mail to yourself, a cloud drive — a file on this phone goes with the phone.

Off. Nothing will be said again when your rules change.

Kept in memory only, never written to disk, and gone when the filter stops. Counters keep working either way.
Malachi installs its own updates from GitHub Releases.

Tested releases. What everyone else gets.
Early builds, as they are written. Expect rough edges.
Testing builds are published as they are written and nobody else has run them yet. Something that works today can break tomorrow, and the filter is what your phone resolves through.

Coming back is not immediate: Android will not install an older version over a newer one, so you would stay on the test build until the stable channel passes it. If you need to return sooner, save a backup of your settings and install the stable APK by hand.
You are on a build newer than the stable channel (%1$s). You will rejoin it at the next stable release.
To return now, save a backup and reinstall the stable version by hand.
Records every lookup and every dropped packet for %1$d minutes, so a problem can be read off the log. In memory only — it is never written to disk and is gone when filtering stops.
Recording. Stops by itself in %1$d min. Open the log below and copy it.

Not checked: updates are set to Wi-Fi only and this connection is metered.
A DNS-level ad and tracker blocker. It runs as a local VPN that carries nothing but DNS: no traffic leaves the phone through Malachi, and nothing is sent anywhere.
Apps using encrypted DNS (DoH or DoT) of their own, unless the bypass guard is set high enough to cut them off.
Content fetched from an IP address with no lookup at all.
Ads served from the same domain as the content around them — DNS cannot tell the two apart.
Anything, while another VPN app is running. Android allows only one.

The handful of addresses your phone uses to check whether a network works. No list may block those: if one did, your phone would decide a perfectly good Wi-Fi had no internet and quietly move to mobile data.
The filter could not start. Trying again shortly.
Another app is set as the always-on VPN, and Android only allows one at a time.
%1$s is set as the always-on VPN. Android will not let Malachi take over until that is turned off in VPN settings.

Set Malachi as your always-on VPN so filtering survives a reboot and no other app can quietly take the VPN slot. Leave “Block connections without VPN” off — Malachi routes only DNS, so that setting would cut off everything else.
Android only runs one VPN at a time. Always-on reserves it for Malachi and brings the filter back after a reboot.
Not set. Filtering still restarts after a reboot, but another VPN app can take over.
%1$s holds it. Malachi cannot run until that changes.
Android refused the VPN permission, so nothing is being filtered. Tap Turn on to try again — or, if that keeps failing, check whether another app is set as your always-on VPN.
Another VPN app is running, and Android allows only one. Accepting Malachi\'s permission will replace it; if it is set as always-on, turn that off in VPN settings first.
Only Android can say whether this is set. Open VPN settings to check or change it.

The apps whose lookups are refused most often. Needs at least %1$d lookups in the period, so a handful of samples can\'t claim 100%%.

When an app hangs or half-loads, watch it and find the domain that has to be excepted.
Pick the app that misbehaves. Malachi will write down every address it asks for, in order, for %1$d minutes — what was refused, what was answered and how long it took. Nothing is saved to the phone.
Watch its lookups one by one and try exceptions until it works.
The window has closed. What it recorded is still here.
Choose a different one to watch. This one\'s timeline is replaced.
Malachi is not filtering right now, so it can\'t see anything this app asks for.
%1$s is outside the filter, so its lookups never reach Malachi and nothing will appear here.

Everything refused for this app, most asked for first. The switch allows one here and nowhere else, and takes effect on the very next lookup — no restart. Tap the row instead to cover a parent domain.
Nothing has been refused for this app since you started watching. If it is still failing, a blocked domain is not the cause — look for lookups with no answer below.
Newest first, one line per question the app asked. Your own changes appear here too, so you can see what you have already tried.
Nothing yet. Open %1$s and use the part that fails, then come back.
No DNS server answered — the app waited %1$d ms
Dropped: too many lookups at once

Malachi allows everything it was refusing, then puts the addresses back one at a time and asks you after each. The moment the app breaks again, the one address that is refused is the one to blame. You never have to read a domain until the end.
Open %1$s and do the thing that does not work. Malachi is writing down every address it refuses. Then come back here.

Malachi refused nothing at all for %1$s while you were in it. Either it never got as far as the part that fails, or a blocked address is not the cause — the lookups with no answer, below, are the other thing that hangs an app.
Nothing is being refused for %1$s any more. Force-stop it, open it again and do the same thing. Did it work this time?
Only %1$s is refused now — everything else is allowed. Force-stop %2$s, open it and repeat. Did it work this time?
Force-stopping it matters: Android can hold on to an address for a minute or two after a change, so if an answer surprises you, start the search again.
%1$s is the address that breaks %2$s: with only that one refused, it failed. Allowing it in this app leaves it blocked everywhere else on the phone.
%1$s failed with nothing refused at all, so whatever is wrong with it, Malachi is not what is doing it. Everything is being put back as it was.

Each of the %1$d addresses was refused on its own and %2$s went on working. It may need more than one of them at once, or the failure may not happen every time. Allowing all of them is still far narrower than taking %2$s out of the filter.
%1$d addresses were refused; the search tests the %2$d it was asked for most.
Installing it now. Tap to open Malachi.
An ad and tracker blocker that works for every app on the phone, not just the browser.

Apps ask for an address before they can load anything. Malachi reads those requests and answers the ones that belong to advertising and tracking with nothing, so the advert is never fetched. It is why pages load faster and why apps you never opened stop reporting home.
Why Android will mention a VPN

Android only lets an app see those requests if it registers as a VPN, so in a moment the system will ask you to allow a connection and warn that Malachi “can monitor all network traffic”. That warning is about the permission, not about this app: nothing here leaves your phone, and there is no server on the other end. Malachi is the other end.

Nowhere. There is no account, no analytics and no company. The list of what your phone looked up is kept in memory and disappears when filtering stops; the counters on the home screen are numbers with no names in them. The only things Malachi downloads are the blocklists and its own updates.
